modules.title: Collision detection and physical simulation
modules.project: Build a deterministic test harness for a small physics scene, compare your simple implementation with a maintained physics library, and record precisely which physical and numerical assumptions differ.

lessons.title: Broad phase, narrow phase and geometric robustness
lessons.goal: Separate possible collisions from confirmed contacts.
original_paragraphs: A collision system first identifies potentially interacting pairs, then performs more expensive geometric tests. The broad phase must be conservative: extra candidate pairs cost time, but missing a real collision breaks correctness. Spatial grids, sweep-and-prune and bounding-volume hierarchies suit different distributions and movement patterns.

The narrow phase determines actual overlap or separation and, when needed, contact positions and normals. Contact normal orientation is an interface contract. Touching, overlapping and nearly parallel configurations need deliberate tolerance policies. Floating-point tolerances should relate to scale and purpose, not an unexplained universal constant. Keep a brute-force pair generator as an oracle for small tests before optimizing.
Implement a grid broad phase and circle or box narrow phase. Pass: no true pairs are omitted compared with brute force over randomized scenes, and boundary-touching behavior is documented.
R28: collision module, shapes and broad-phase concepts; R19: geometry and collision.
lessons.original_example: For 100 objects, checking every unordered pair requires 100 x 99 / 2 = 4,950 pair tests. A broad phase helps only if its maintenance cost and candidate count are favorable for the scene.
lessons.original_lab: Implement a grid broad phase and circle or box narrow phase. Pass: no true pairs are omitted compared with brute force over randomized scenes, and boundary-touching behavior is documented.
lessons.original_reading: R28 : collision module, shapes and broad-phase concepts; R19 : geometry and collision.
original_questions: May a correct broad phase return false positives?
How many unordered pairs exist for 100 objects?
Why document contact-normal orientation?
original_answers: Yes. Narrow-phase tests can reject them; false negatives are the dangerous case.
Impulse and separation calculations depend on a consistent direction between the two bodies.

lessons.title: Rigid bodies, angular motion and collision impulses
lessons.goal: Use conservation laws with explicit approximations.
original_paragraphs: A rigid-body model represents position, orientation, linear velocity and angular velocity without modeling deformation. Mass relates force to linear acceleration, while an inertia tensor relates torque and angular acceleration under the chosen frame conventions. Off-center forces and impulses can change rotation as well as translation.

Collision impulses change velocity over an idealized short event. For a frictionless one-dimensional collision, restitution controls the ratio of separating to approaching relative speed under the model. Friction constrains tangential impulses and requires care around resting contact. Infinite-mass or static bodies are commonly represented through zero inverse mass rather than numerical infinity. Conservation tests are powerful when applied to scenarios that actually satisfy the assumptions.

Implement center-of-mass impulses and a simple rotational case. Pass: momentum is conserved in isolated tests within tolerance, static bodies remain fixed, and energy behavior matches the chosen restitution model.
R28: rigid bodies, contacts and simulation; R19: physical simulation.
lessons.original_example: A 2 kg body receiving a 6 N*s impulse through its center changes velocity by 3 m/s. The same impulse away from its center also changes angular momentum.
lessons.original_lab: Implement center-of-mass impulses and a simple rotational case. Pass: momentum is conserved in isolated tests within tolerance, static bodies remain fixed, and energy behavior matches the chosen restitution model.
lessons.original_reading: R28 : rigid bodies, contacts and simulation; R19 : physical simulation.
original_questions: What velocity change follows from 6 N*s applied to 2 kg?
Why can an off-center impulse cause rotation?
Why use zero inverse mass for a static body?
original_answers: 3 m/s in the impulse direction.
It changes angular momentum through the lever arm relative to the center of mass.
It naturally produces no velocity change under impulse calculations without relying on infinite numerical values.

lessons.title: Constraints, iterative solvers and continuous collision detection
lessons.goal: Explain where discrete simulation fails and how solvers control error.
original_paragraphs: A constraint restricts allowed motion, such as maintaining a joint distance or preventing interpenetration. Iterative solvers repeatedly reduce constraint error using local updates. The number of iterations, ordering, timestep and warm starting influence convergence and apparent stiffness. A stable-looking scene is not proof of exact constraint satisfaction.

Discrete collision detection samples configurations at steps and can miss an object passing completely through a thin obstacle. Continuous methods examine motion over an interval or estimate a time of impact. They require motion assumptions and add cost. Use them selectively where speed and geometry justify them. Position correction should not silently create unbounded energy or conceal a broken velocity solver.

Create a fast-projectile tunneling test and a short chain of constraints. Pass: a continuous or swept test catches the projectile, and a plot or table shows constraint error versus iteration count and timestep.
R28: joints, solver settings and continuous collision; R19: numerical simulation.
lessons.original_example: An object moving 30 m/s travels 0.5 m during a 1/60 s step. A wall much thinner than that can be crossed between sampled positions without either endpoint overlapping.
lessons.original_lab: Create a fast-projectile tunneling test and a short chain of constraints. Pass: a continuous or swept test catches the projectile, and a plot or table shows constraint error versus iteration count and timestep.
lessons.original_reading: R28 : joints, solver settings and continuous collision; R19 : numerical simulation.
original_questions: How far does 30 m/s travel in 1/60 second?
Why can increasing solver iterations help?
Does CCD remove every numerical simulation problem?
original_answers: It can reduce residual constraint error, though cost rises and other modeling problems can remain.
No. It addresses certain between-step collision failures under its motion and solver assumptions.

lessons.title: Physics testing, determinism and engine integration
lessons.goal: Validate simulation with invariants and adversarial scenes.
original_paragraphs: Physics tests should include resting stacks, extreme but supported mass ratios, repeated contacts, long runtimes and objects entering or leaving the world. Define units and supported scales before tuning. NaNs or exploding positions should produce a diagnostic near their origin, not only a later renderer crash.

Deterministic replay requires control of ordering, arithmetic assumptions, random sources and inputs. Bitwise determinism across platforms is a stronger requirement than visually similar behavior on one machine. A library can have explicit determinism limits; record them. Compare analytic solutions where available and use convergence studies elsewhere. Integration tests must verify that rendering interpolation, collision events and entity destruction do not violate the physics system's lifetime rules.

Build a regression suite with replay hashes on one pinned environment, finite-value checks and analytic tests. Pass: failures identify the first divergent tick and reports distinguish same-machine repeatability from cross-platform determinism.
R28: simulation, determinism and limitations; revisit Modules 08 and 24.
lessons.original_example: A freely moving body with no force should maintain velocity in the ideal model. A falling body before collision can be checked against an analytic constant-acceleration solution, separating integration error from collision behavior.
lessons.original_lab: Build a regression suite with replay hashes on one pinned environment, finite-value checks and analytic tests. Pass: failures identify the first divergent tick and reports distinguish same-machine repeatability from cross-platform determinism.
lessons.original_reading: R28 : simulation, determinism and limitations; revisit Modules 08 and 24.

Why identify the first divergent tick?
What should happen when a simulation first creates a NaN?
original_answers: No. Compiler, arithmetic and implementation differences can still matter.
It localizes the origin of disagreement before later effects amplify it.
Capture a useful diagnostic and reject or isolate invalid state according to policy rather than letting it propagate silently.

modules.title: Animation, audio and interactive timing
modules.project: Integrate an animated character or articulated object with event-driven audio. Demonstrate smooth interpolation, bounded audio work, adjustable sound categories and correct behavior when animation rate differs from simulation rate.

lessons.title: Skeletons, transforms and skinning
lessons.goal: Compute hierarchical animation without mixing coordinate spaces.
original_paragraphs: A skeleton is a hierarchy of local transforms. A joint's world transform depends on its ancestors, so evaluation must respect the hierarchy. Skinning transforms mesh vertices using joint transforms and stored bind information. Inverse bind matrices relate the original mesh pose to the current skeleton; applying a transform in the wrong space creates characteristic stretching or displacement.

Linear blend skinning combines transformed positions using weights that normally sum to one. It is efficient but has deformation limitations. Rotations should be interpolated with a representation appropriate to orientation, such as normalized quaternions with a shortest-path convention. Interpolating arbitrary matrix entries can introduce unintended scale or shear. Test a two-joint example before importing a complex character.
Animate a two-joint mesh or line skeleton. Pass: the bind pose reproduces the source geometry, weights are validated and a parent rotation moves descendants consistently.
R19: transformations and animation; R26: skeletal animation concepts.
lessons.original_example: A vertex influenced equally by two joints has weights 0.5 and 0.5. Omitting the bind-pose correction can move it even when the skeleton is supposedly in its original pose.
lessons.original_lab: Animate a two-joint mesh or line skeleton. Pass: the bind pose reproduces the source geometry, weights are validated and a parent rotation moves descendants consistently.
lessons.original_reading: R19 : transformations and animation; R26 : skeletal animation concepts.

What should ordinary normalized skinning weights sum to?
Why avoid directly interpolating arbitrary rotation-matrix entries?
original_answers: A child world transform depends on the parent world transform.
One.

lessons.title: Animation blending, state machines and inverse kinematics
lessons.goal: Coordinate authored motion with runtime goals.
original_paragraphs: Animation state machines choose motion states and transitions, while blend systems combine clips using parameters such as speed or direction. Transition conditions, interruption rules and event timing are part of gameplay behavior. A clip completing is not always equivalent to an action becoming interruptible.

Inverse kinematics finds joint configurations that satisfy target constraints, such as placing a foot on a surface. It may have no solution, multiple solutions or a solution outside joint limits. Iterative methods need stopping criteria and stable behavior near unreachable targets. Root motion introduces a policy decision about whether animation or simulation controls displacement. Keep ownership clear to prevent animation and physics from both moving the same body inconsistently.
Build idle/walk/action transitions and a two-link IK demonstration. Pass: interruptions behave as specified, unreachable targets are handled, and root-motion ownership is documented.
R19: animation and inverse kinematics; R26: animation blueprints and blending concepts, compared with your own small implementation.
lessons.original_example: A two-link arm with lengths 1 and 1 cannot reach a target 3 units from its base. A solver should clamp or report the unreachable condition rather than generating invalid angles.
lessons.original_lab: Build idle/walk/action transitions and a two-link IK demonstration. Pass: interruptions behave as specified, unreachable targets are handled, and root-motion ownership is documented.

What is the maximum reach of two collinear links of length 1 each?
Why define root-motion ownership?
original_answers: No. Geometry, joint limits and constraints can make targets unreachable.
2 units.

lessons.title: Digital audio, mixing and real-time callback discipline
lessons.goal: Generate sound without missing the output deadline.
original_paragraphs: Digital audio represents sampled signals. Sample rate, channel layout and sample format describe the buffer contract. Mixing combines signals with controlled gain; clipping occurs when output exceeds the representable or intended range. Resampling is a signal-processing operation requiring filtering, not merely dropping arbitrary samples.

An audio callback usually has a deadline tied to the buffer duration. Avoid unbounded allocation, blocking locks, disk access or unpredictable work on that path. Prepare data elsewhere and communicate through a carefully designed bounded mechanism. Smaller buffers can reduce one source of latency but leave less scheduling margin. Measure underruns and end-to-end response rather than assuming the smallest available buffer is best.
Mix two generated tones with adjustable gains using a platform audio API. Pass: no clipping under the documented gain policy, bounded callback work and a recorded underrun or deadline-stress test.
R10 from Volume 2: sampling and filtering; R22: SDL3 audio; R20: audio systems.
lessons.original_example: A 256-frame buffer at 48,000 frames per second spans 256/48,000 seconds, about 5.33 ms. A callback that blocks for 20 ms can miss that timing requirement.
lessons.original_lab: Mix two generated tones with adjustable gains using a platform audio API. Pass: no clipping under the documented gain policy, bounded callback work and a recorded underrun or deadline-stress test.

Why avoid disk reads inside an audio callback?

original_answers: Approximately 5.33 ms.
Their unpredictable blocking time can exceed the audio deadline.
No. It can reduce buffering latency while increasing deadline pressure and underrun risk.

lessons.title: Spatial audio, animation events and multimodal accessibility
lessons.goal: Synchronize feedback while preserving user control.
original_paragraphs: Spatial audio approximates cues such as level, direction and environmental filtering. A simple stereo pan is not a full head-related acoustic model. Distance attenuation and occlusion are design choices that should be consistent with the game's spatial scale and readability needs. Avoid treating physically plausible sound as automatically useful feedback.

Animation and gameplay events should reference a deliberate clock and deduplication policy. Rollback or repeated evaluation must not replay every sound unintentionally. Provide category volume controls and alternatives for information communicated only through sound or color. Subtitle timing, speaker identification and visual event indicators are engineering requirements, not a final decoration. Evaluate accessibility with actual task completion where possible.

Add spatial panning, separate music/effects controls and a visual equivalent for a critical audio cue. Pass: replay does not duplicate one-shot events and a muted-audio test still allows the required task.
R20: audio and event systems; R22: audio interfaces; R29 from the resource directory: audio and subtitle accessibility.
lessons.original_example: A predicted footstep may be encountered again during replay. Assigning an event identity and a presentation policy prevents an unintended duplicate sound while preserving the corrected simulation.
lessons.original_lab: Add spatial panning, separate music/effects controls and a visual equivalent for a critical audio cue. Pass: replay does not duplicate one-shot events and a muted-audio test still allows the required task.

Why give presentation events stable identities during replay?

original_answers: No. It represents only some directional cues.

modules.title: Game AI, decision systems and machine learning
modules.project: Build an inspectable agent that navigates, chooses actions and recovers from blocked plans. Compare a rules-based baseline with one small learned or search-based component; evaluate behavior and runtime cost, not only win rate.

lessons.title: Navigation graphs, steering and dynamic obstacles
lessons.goal: Separate finding a route from executing movement.
original_paragraphs: Pathfinding chooses a route through an abstract representation; steering controls local motion along or toward that route. A navigation mesh represents traversable regions, while grids and waypoint graphs offer other tradeoffs. The abstraction must include the agent's dimensions and movement constraints. A path valid for a point may be impossible for a wide character.

Dynamic obstacles can invalidate a route or require local avoidance. Replanning every frame for every agent may waste time; never replanning may leave agents stuck. Use bounded work, event-driven invalidation and observable failure states. Local avoidance does not guarantee a globally feasible route. Test narrow passages, opposing traffic and unreachable destinations rather than only empty rooms.
Combine A* with a steering controller and a blocked-path detector. Pass: agent size is respected, unreachable goals terminate or report failure, and repeated replanning has a bounded budget.
R46: Search; R20: game AI and navigation concepts.
lessons.original_example: A doorway 0.8 units wide is not traversable by a circular agent with diameter 1.0 under a no-overlap model, even if the navigation graph contains an edge through its center.
lessons.original_lab: Combine A* with a steering controller and a blocked-path detector. Pass: agent size is respected, unreachable goals terminate or report failure, and repeated replanning has a bounded budget.
lessons.original_reading: R46 : Search; R20 : game AI and navigation concepts.

Can the example 1.0-wide agent pass through the 0.8-wide doorway?
Why bound replanning work?
original_answers: Pathfinding selects a route; steering produces local movement to follow or adjust that route.

lessons.title: Behavior trees, utility systems and explainable decisions
lessons.goal: Represent behavior so designers can understand its failures.
original_paragraphs: A finite-state machine encodes states and transitions. A behavior tree organizes conditional execution and action status. A utility system scores alternatives and selects according to a policy. These are alternative or complementary organizational tools, not a ranking from obsolete to modern. Choose based on behavior complexity, authoring needs and debugging.

An action should expose progress, success, failure and cancellation semantics. Utility scores need compatible scales and often hysteresis to prevent rapid switching between nearly equal options. Behavior traces should record why an action was selected and why it failed. A black-box agent that occasionally behaves well is harder to improve than a simpler agent whose decisions can be inspected.
Implement either a small behavior tree or utility selector with a trace viewer. Pass: action cancellation releases resources and three induced failure cases produce understandable explanations.
R20: game AI; R46: agents, utilities and decision-making foundations.
lessons.original_example: An agent choosing between attack score 0.51 and retreat score 0.50 can oscillate as small observations change. A switching threshold or minimum commitment interval can stabilize the policy, with explicit tradeoffs.
lessons.original_lab: Implement either a small behavior tree or utility selector with a trace viewer. Pass: action cancellation releases resources and three induced failure cases produce understandable explanations.
lessons.original_reading: R20 : game AI; R46 : agents, utilities and decision-making foundations.

Why can nearly tied utility scores cause oscillation?
Why is a decision trace valuable?
original_answers: At least a defined running/progress state, success, failure and cancellation behavior.

lessons.title: Adversarial search, planning and simulation budgets
lessons.goal: Trade decision quality against bounded computation.
original_paragraphs: Minimax reasons about alternating choices under a specified game model. Alpha-beta pruning can avoid exploring branches that cannot affect the result while preserving the minimax value under the same assumptions. Move ordering changes efficiency, not the objective. Evaluation functions approximate the value of states that cannot be searched to completion.

Monte Carlo tree search uses repeated sampled exploration to allocate work. Its behavior depends on sampling, exploration policy and rollout or value estimates. Real-time agents need deadlines and a valid fallback action. Hidden information requires reasoning about beliefs rather than granting the agent access to facts a player could not observe. Compare policies on diverse scenarios, not only against one weak opponent.

Implement minimax with alpha-beta or a small MCTS agent for a tiny game. Pass: legal moves are always returned within a defined budget or fallback, and evaluation includes multiple seeds and opponents.
R46: Games, Minimax, Expectimax and Monte Carlo Tree Search.
lessons.original_example: A branching factor of 10 searched to depth 6 can produce roughly one million leaf paths before pruning. A 2 ms decision budget cannot be assumed sufficient without measurement and a bounded policy.
lessons.original_lab: Implement minimax with alpha-beta or a small MCTS agent for a tiny game. Pass: legal moves are always returned within a defined budget or fallback, and evaluation includes multiple seeds and opponents.
lessons.original_reading: R46 : Games, Minimax, Expectimax and Monte Carlo Tree Search.

How many depth-6 paths arise from branching factor 10 without pruning?
Why use a fallback action?
original_answers: No. It prunes branches that cannot affect the same result under the search assumptions.

The decision deadline may arrive before the planned search completes.

lessons.title: Learning systems, neural inference and responsible evaluation
lessons.goal: Understand learning fundamentals without replacing every subsystem with a model.
original_paragraphs: Supervised learning fits parameters from examples; reinforcement learning optimizes behavior through rewards and interaction. A training objective is not the same as the desired player experience. Split data by independent episodes or sources when appropriate so nearly duplicate examples do not leak between training and testing. Establish a simple non-learned baseline first.

A neural network composes parameterized transformations and nonlinearities; gradients update parameters through the chain rule. Inference cost includes preprocessing, memory movement and scheduling, not only arithmetic. Distribution shift can cause failure when gameplay differs from training. Record data rights, privacy and failure policies. Learned components should remain bounded and observable, especially when their output affects authoritative game state.

Train a small classifier or value estimator on synthetic game data and compare it with a rules baseline. Pass: independent splits, error analysis, inference timing, reproducible seeds and a fallback behavior are reported.
R46: Machine Learning and Reinforcement Learning; R47: linear models, multilayer perceptrons, backpropagation and generalization.
lessons.original_example: A model trained and tested on adjacent frames from the same recorded match may appear accurate by exploiting near-duplicates. Holding out complete matches provides a stronger test of generalization.
lessons.original_lab: Train a small classifier or value estimator on synthetic game data and compare it with a rules baseline. Pass: independent splits, error analysis, inference timing, reproducible seeds and a fallback behavior are reported.

What mathematical rule underlies backpropagation?

original_answers: It reduces leakage from highly correlated examples belonging to the same episode.

modules.title: Multiplayer simulation and online services

modules.project: Create a local two-client multiplayer demonstration with a network simulator for delay, jitter, loss, duplication and reordering. No public server or paid cloud account is required. Document authority and recovery rules.

lessons.title: Authority, prediction and reconciliation
lessons.goal: Provide responsive local control without trusting arbitrary client outcomes.
original_paragraphs: An authoritative simulation decides which state is accepted as game truth. Clients commonly send input intentions rather than unrestricted final positions or rewards. Local prediction improves immediate response by simulating the client's own input before server confirmation. Reconciliation compares authoritative state with the corresponding predicted history and reapplies unacknowledged inputs when necessary.

Input sequence numbers or simulation ticks make this correspondence possible. Validation needs resource and rate limits as well as semantic checks. Authority does not eliminate all cheating or fairness problems, but it defines the trust boundary. Presentation smoothing should not rewrite the authoritative rules. Keep correction behavior visible during development so errors are not merely hidden behind interpolation.
Implement a one-dimensional or grid movement server with client prediction. Pass: invalid movement is rejected and induced delay produces documented corrections without permanently diverging state.
R17: transport semantics; R26: networking and multiplayer concepts; R20: networking in games.

lessons.title: Snapshots, interpolation, relevance and lag compensation
lessons.goal: Manage bandwidth and latency while making fairness assumptions explicit.
original_paragraphs: Remote entities can be rendered between buffered snapshots, trading some added presentation delay for smoother motion under jitter. Extrapolation predicts beyond available data and can be wrong when motion changes. Snapshot sequence numbers, timestamps and baselines must be validated. Delta compression requires agreement about the baseline being referenced.

Interest management sends relevant state rather than every entity to every client. Relevance is also a security concern: sending hidden information can expose it even when the interface does not display it. Lag compensation may evaluate an action against historical state, but history bounds and fairness policy must be explicit. There is no universal policy that makes every latency condition equally fair.

Add remote interpolation and relevance filtering. Pass: out-of-order snapshots are handled, missing baselines trigger recovery, and the report explains both visual delay and hidden-state exposure policy.
R20: networked game state; R26: replication and network smoothing; revisit Module 19 message validation.

lessons.original_lab: Add remote interpolation and relevance filtering. Pass: out-of-order snapshots are handled, missing baselines trigger recovery, and the report explains both visual delay and hidden-state exposure policy.

lessons.title: Lockstep, rollback and deterministic replay
lessons.goal: Choose synchronization around the game model rather than genre slogans.
original_paragraphs: Lockstep peers or participants advance a deterministic simulation using agreed inputs. It can reduce state bandwidth, but progress depends on input availability and determinism. A single divergent arithmetic or ordering decision can amplify into different worlds. Periodic state hashes help detect disagreement but do not repair it by themselves.

Rollback predicts missing inputs, then restores a past state and resimulates when the prediction differs. It needs fast state capture, bounded history and careful handling of irreversible presentation or external side effects. The rollback horizon controls memory and correction cost. Neither rollback nor lockstep is automatically appropriate for every RTS or action game; evaluate state size, simulation cost, latency and player experience.

Implement rollback or input lockstep for the tiny deterministic game. Pass: a delayed-input test converges, state hashes detect a deliberately introduced divergence, and audio or reward side effects are not duplicated.
R20 and R26: multiplayer concepts; derive the implementation using Modules 18, 24 and 26 rather than assuming engine-specific guarantees.

lessons.title: Match services, identity, persistence and failure recovery
lessons.goal: Design a small online service without treating it as part of the render loop.
original_paragraphs: Matchmaking, authentication, session allocation and persistent progression are service responsibilities distinct from frame simulation. A match can continue or fail under a defined policy when a nonessential service is unavailable. Identity and authorization must be checked at the relevant boundary; a valid account is not permission to modify another account's data.

Retries, timeouts and idempotency are essential for reward and progression operations. Use established authentication and cryptographic libraries rather than inventing protocols. Store secrets outside repositories and logs. Operational readiness includes health checks, structured diagnostics, graceful shutdown and recovery tests. For learning, local mock services and synthetic accounts are sufficient and avoid unnecessary privacy and spending risks.

Build a local match registry and idempotent result store. Pass: duplicate submissions do not duplicate rewards, unauthorized edits fail, and simulated service loss produces a documented client outcome.

modules.title: Production quality and the undergraduate engine capstone
modules.prerequisites: Modules 21-29 plus Gate D software-engineering evidence.

lessons.title: Profiling, frame budgets and performance regression tests
lessons.goal: Optimize measured bottlenecks without sacrificing correctness.
original_paragraphs: Profiling identifies where time and resources are spent under a specific workload. Instrumentation records explicit events; sampling estimates where execution tends to be observed. Both have overhead and interpretation limits. A CPU trace alone cannot fully explain GPU work, and a GPU timing alone cannot describe input-to-display latency.

Create repeatable scenes with fixed settings and a warmup policy. Record build type, hardware, drivers, resolution and background conditions. Measure distributions and peak memory, then change one hypothesis-driven factor at a time. A microbenchmark speedup is useful only if it improves an important application path without unacceptable regressions. Keep correctness tests alongside performance tests and tolerate normal measurement noise appropriately.

Profile the capstone scene, optimize one verified bottleneck and add a regression benchmark. Pass: repeated before/after results, unchanged correctness and disclosed measurement uncertainty are included.
R26: profiling and optimization; R45: sanitizer diagnostics; revisit Modules 09 and 18.

lessons.title: Compatibility, accessibility, localization and human testing
lessons.goal: Test whether people can actually use the complete product.
original_paragraphs: A compatibility matrix lists supported environments and input/display configurations. Test cases should include different resolutions, aspect ratios, controllers, keyboard layouts and missing optional devices where relevant. Unsupported cases need clear behavior rather than accidental crashes. Localization affects text length, fonts, layout, number formatting and sometimes text direction.

Accessibility begins with requirements such as remappable controls, readable interface scale, contrast, alternative cues and adjustable timing where the game permits. A guideline checklist supports design but does not replace user testing or establish legal compliance. Use informed, voluntary test participation and collect only necessary data. Observe task completion and confusion rather than asking only whether the game is enjoyable.

Test the game at two window sizes, with remapped input and an expanded pseudo-localized text set. Pass: no critical clipped controls, a muted-audio task remains solvable and observed usability issues are tracked.
R29: input, text, audio, contrast and UI guidelines; R20: playtesting and production.
lessons.original_example: A button sized for a short English label can clip a longer translated label. A control prompt that hard-codes a keyboard letter can become wrong after rebinding.
lessons.original_lab: Test the game at two window sizes, with remapped input and an expanded pseudo-localized text set. Pass: no critical clipped controls, a muted-audio task remains solvable and observed usability issues are tracked.

The current binding, not an obsolete hard-coded default.
No. It supports engineering review but is not a legal determination or substitute for user evaluation.

lessons.title: Packaging, patching, modding and supply-chain boundaries
lessons.goal: Distribute a game without creating an uncontrolled execution path.
original_paragraphs: A release package includes the executable, required runtime assets, dependency information, notices and configuration defaults. Test installation and startup outside the development tree. Patch systems need integrity checks, version compatibility and a rollback or recovery plan; interrupted updates must not destroy the only runnable installation.

Modding expands the trust boundary. Data-only mods still require parsing and resource limits, while executable plugins can run with substantial authority unless isolated. Define supported APIs, compatibility versions and permissions. Do not download and execute arbitrary community code automatically. A script sandbox needs explicit capability and resource limits, and its security depends on implementation, not the word sandbox. Preserve user saves separately from replaceable program files.

Package the game and implement a data-only mod with a versioned schema. Pass: a clean-folder launch works, oversized or malformed mods are rejected and an interrupted-update simulation preserves a valid version.
R20: production; R26: packaging and plugins; R45 and Module 20: defensive memory and dependency practices.
lessons.original_example: A malformed mod declares a texture with dimensions large enough to overflow a byte-count calculation. Validation must check multiplication and total resource limits before allocation, even though the file is nominally data.
lessons.original_lab: Package the game and implement a data-only mod with a versioned schema. Pass: a clean-folder launch works, oversized or malformed mods are rejected and an interrupted-update simulation preserves a valid version.

Why separate saves from replaceable installation files?
Does naming a system a sandbox establish isolation?
original_answers: Yes. Malformed sizes, structures or resource demands can trigger failures unless validated.
Updates or reinstalls should not erase user progress.
No. Isolation depends on the enforced capability, memory and resource boundaries.

lessons.title: Capstone review, release and technical postmortem
lessons.goal: Demonstrate ownership of a complete engineering result.
original_paragraphs: A capstone combines requirements, implementation, tests, performance evidence and communication. Freeze a small scope: one complete loop with a clear beginning, success/failure and restart is enough. Review the architecture against actual use, not only the original diagram. List dependencies and distinguish original code from libraries or assistance.

A technical postmortem explains what worked, what failed, evidence behind decisions and what would change next. Avoid rewriting the project history as an uninterrupted success story. An oral review should include a live bug investigation, a design tradeoff and a small code modification. These reveal understanding beyond a polished video. Graduation to advanced work requires the practical artifact and reasoning, not only lesson attendance.

Complete Gate F and the oral questions in the handbook. Pass: another tester finishes a full loop, the release is reproducible, critical defects are resolved or clearly blocked from release, and the postmortem cites measured evidence.
R20: course projects and critique; revisit the project rubric and professional-practice lessons.
lessons.original_example: A small game with reproducible builds, bounded memory, clear controls and an honest bug list is stronger evidence of engineering ownership than an unfinished large world with no tests.
lessons.original_lab: Complete Gate F and the oral questions in the handbook. Pass: another tester finishes a full loop, the release is reproducible, critical defects are resolved or clearly blocked from release, and the postmortem cites measured evidence.
lessons.original_reading: R20 : course projects and critique; revisit the project rubric and professional-practice lessons.

Why disclose library and AI assistance?
Why include a live modification in an oral review?
original_answers: A reproducible package, tests, usable controls, documented limitations and independent execution.
It distinguishes the learner's decisions and understanding from supplied work and supports provenance.
It tests whether the learner can reason about and change the system rather than only present a prepared artifact.

26.1.body:
### The engineering problem
A projectile passes through a door only when the camera looks away. Before changing an epsilon, determine which subsystem owns collision membership and whether its update depends on rendering. Collision is simulation work. A visibility optimization must not remove an object from the collision world. Write the contract first: positions are meters, axes are right-handed in the simulation, AABBs are closed intervals, and normals point from body A toward body B.

### Broad phase is a conservative filter
For n objects, exhaustive testing considers n(n-1)/2 unordered pairs. With 100 objects this is 4,950. Keep that implementation as an independent oracle. An optimized broad phase is correct when every truly overlapping pair is a candidate. It may return extra candidates. Comparing candidate sets for equality is therefore the wrong test; compare true contacts against the candidate superset, then compare narrow-phase results.

A uniform grid inserts each object's complete bounding box into every cell it overlaps. Compute a cell coordinate with floor(x/cell_size), not integer truncation toward zero. An object crossing the origin reveals the difference. Insert a closed box's maximum boundary conservatively even when it lies exactly on a cell edge. Emit canonical pairs (min_id, max_id), deduplicate them, and sort before the solver consumes them. Inserting only the center is not conservative for objects larger than a cell.

Grid performance depends on occupancy and object size. A crowded cell can still contain almost every pair. A huge object can occupy thousands of cells. Keep membership and pair counts in the profiler; a data structure name does not imply a speedup. A dynamic AABB tree is an alternative for heterogeneous sizes, while sweep-and-prune can exploit coherence along an axis. Box2D's collision documentation provides maintained shape queries and a dynamic-tree comparison target [S01].

### Narrow phase and the meaning of contact
For circles, let d = center_B - center_A and R = radius_A + radius_B. Overlap under our closed-set policy means dot(d,d) <= R*R. Only after this decision do we need a square root for distance and a normalized contact normal. If the centers coincide, dividing by distance is invalid. Choose a deterministic fallback normal, such as the previous valid normal or a stable axis derived from IDs, and document it.

For AABBs, reject the pair when either axis separates the intervals. For convex polygons, the separating-axis theorem motivates projecting both polygons onto candidate edge normals: a separating interval proves no overlap. Absence of separation is not yet a complete contact manifold. Concave meshes need decomposition or a different representation. Do not present the circle lab as a finished general-purpose collision library.

### Worked trace: a cell boundary that breaks naive code
Let cell size be 1 m. Circle A has center (-0.1, 0), radius 0.2 m; circle B has center (0.15, 0), radius 0.1 m. Their center distance is 0.25 m and their radius sum is 0.3 m, so they overlap. A's x bounds are [-0.3, 0.1], spanning cells -1 and 0. B's bounds are [0.05, 0.25], in cell 0. Both also span y cells -1 and 0. A center-only or incorrectly truncated implementation can conceal a missing-cell defect in other placements. The robust implementation inserts full bounds and deduplicates shared-cell pairs.

Translate this entire scene by exactly 10 m and repeat. Geometry should be unchanged within the declared numeric tolerance. Repeat with a coincident center, an exact tangent and a radius near the minimum supported scale. These are different questions: boundary policy, degeneracy policy and scale policy must not be collapsed into one unexplained constant.

### Implementation and debugging discipline
```text
validate finite coordinates and positive cell size
for each stable body ID:
    compute shape AABB
    insert ID into every covered cell
for each occupied cell:
    emit all distinct ID pairs in canonical order
sort and unique candidates
run narrow phase; record contact IDs and normals
```

In a debug capture, retain bounds, cell memberships, candidate IDs and final contacts for the first missed pair. If a collision disappears, this trace identifies whether membership, filtering, geometry or lifetime failed. Reject invalid geometry before indexing it. Bound object size and cell coverage before allocating storage for user-authored scenes.

### Deliberate practice
First solve the pair calculation on paper. Then implement the exercise kernel without reading its reference. The full lab adds a seeded randomized oracle comparison and an engine-owned spatial index. Measure uniform, clustered and one-giant-object scenes. A correct but slower grid is an acceptable finding; report it rather than choosing a convenient scene after seeing results.
extra_questions: With 250 bodies, how many exhaustive unordered pairs are possible? What relationship must hold between true-contact and candidate sets?
A circle spans four cells but its center occupies one. Is center-only insertion sufficient? Give a repair and a duplicate-pair policy.
extra_answers: 250 x 249 / 2 = 31,125. Every true-contact pair must occur in the candidate set; the reverse inclusion is unnecessary. Extra candidates are a cost, not a correctness defect.
No. A neighbor can intersect the circle outside its center cell. Insert its complete bounding box into every intersected cell, emit canonical body-ID pairs, and deduplicate before applying impulses.

26.1.transfer: Port the broad-phase ownership and pair-order contract into the Volume 5 engine. Keep the brute-force oracle in a debug/headless target, independent of the grid implementation.

26.2.body:
### State, units and approximation
A rigid body has a center-of-mass position, orientation, linear velocity, angular velocity, mass and inertia. A two-dimensional body has scalar angular velocity around the perpendicular axis. In three dimensions, angular velocity is a vector and inertia is a tensor whose frame matters. This lesson derives a 2D contact; the same conceptual separation between translation and rotation carries forward to 3D.

Force has units kg*m/s^2 and changes momentum over time. Impulse has units kg*m/s and changes velocity immediately in the model. Applying a force as an impulse every tick makes behavior depend on tick rate. Conversely, multiplying an already integrated impulse by dt weakens it incorrectly. Keep distinct API names: apply_force and apply_impulse. Static bodies use zero inverse mass and zero inverse inertia, not a floating-point infinity.

### Deriving the contact impulse
Choose a unit normal n from A to B. Let r_A and r_B run from the bodies' centers of mass to the contact. The relative contact-point velocity is v_B + omega_B cross r_B - v_A - omega_A cross r_A. Its projection v_n on n is negative when the bodies approach under this convention. An impulse +j*n goes to B and -j*n to A. For a frictionless instantaneous collision:

```text
k = inv_mass_A + inv_mass_B
    + (cross(r_A,n))^2 * inv_inertia_A
    + (cross(r_B,n))^2 * inv_inertia_B
j = -(1 + restitution) * v_n / k
```

Apply this only to an approaching contact with positive effective inverse mass k. For a separating contact, a positive bounce impulse would manufacture energy. The rotational terms explain why the same contact force can produce different linear outcomes at different lever arms. A normal is a direction, not a penetration distance; normalize it before using these equations.

For a center-of-mass one-dimensional collision, the rotational terms disappear. Equal masses m = 2 kg start at v_A = 3 m/s and v_B = 0. With restitution e = 0.5, relative velocity is -3 m/s, k = 1 kg^-1, and j = 4.5 N*s. The final velocities are 0.75 and 2.25 m/s. Momentum remains 6 kg*m/s. Initial kinetic energy is 9 J and final energy is 5.625 J. The energy loss is expected in this inelastic model, not a failed conservation test.

### Worked rotational impulse
An isolated 2 kg body receives J = (6,0) N*s at offset r = (0,0.5) m. Its linear velocity changes by (3,0) m/s. Angular impulse is cross(r,J) = -3 kg*m^2/s. With inertia 0.25 kg*m^2, angular velocity changes by -12 rad/s. The sign follows the stated right-handed convention. If the application and renderer disagree about vertical-axis direction, the same physical clockwise motion may appear with an inverted screen angle; fix the transform boundary rather than negating impulses opportunistically.

### Friction, resting contacts and energy
A tangential impulse opposes relative sliding. A simple Coulomb constraint bounds its magnitude by mu times the accumulated normal impulse. In an iterative solver, clamp the accumulated tangential impulse, then apply only the increment. Clamping each increment independently can exceed the intended total friction bound. Static and kinetic friction are richer than this compact approximation, especially around transitions and rolling contact.

Restitution is a collision-event model, not a demand that a resting stack bounce every tick. Many engines use a velocity threshold or solver-specific treatment. Study the selected library's contact and material behavior rather than assuming a universal parameter mapping [S02]. Gravity and the floor supply external forces and impulses, so momentum of only the falling body is not conserved. Select an isolated two-body scene when testing total momentum.

### Failure analysis and integration
Check finite state, nonnegative inverse masses, supported restitution and inertia before applying impulses. A static-static contact has zero effective inverse mass and must not divide by zero. Distinguish a dynamic body temporarily at rest from a truly static body. Do not set inverse mass to zero merely because its current velocity is small.

The kernel lab handles center-of-mass velocity updates. The full lab must add the off-center case above, momentum and energy tables, an immovable wall, and tests across at least two fixed timesteps for sustained forces. Integrate through stable body handles. Queue creation and destruction outside solver iteration so callbacks cannot invalidate the contact list.
extra_questions: Two 2 kg bodies have velocities 3 and 0 m/s and restitution 0.5. Compute impulse, final velocities and total final kinetic energy.
A 6 N*s horizontal impulse acts 0.5 m above the center of a body with inertia 0.25 kg*m^2. What angular-velocity change results?
extra_answers: With n from A to B, relative speed is -3, effective inverse mass is 1, and j = 4.5 N*s. A ends at 0.75 m/s; B at 2.25 m/s. Final kinetic energy is 0.5*2*(0.75^2+2.25^2) = 5.625 J. Momentum remains 6 kg*m/s.
Using r=(0,0.5) and J=(6,0), cross(r,J)=-3 kg*m^2/s, so delta omega=-3/0.25=-12 rad/s. Reversing the stated axis convention changes the represented sign, not the physical motion.
26.2.reading: Read S02: rigid bodies, mass data, forces and impulses, friction and restitution. Re-derive the center-contact impulse without copying the supplied equation.
26.2.transfer: Implement separate force and impulse commands in your engine. Add tests proving that the renderer cannot directly overwrite the physics-owned transform of a dynamic body.

26.3.body:
### Two distinct sources of error
A projectile can miss a wall because collision was sampled only at endpoints. A chain can stretch because its constraint solver stopped before convergence. Increasing solver iterations addresses the second problem but does not necessarily discover the missing collision in the first. Diagnose detection, integration and constraint solving independently.

A distance constraint between particles A and B has residual C = length(x_B-x_A) - rest_length. A residual is a measured violation, not a visual impression. For a nonzero separation direction n and inverse masses w_A, w_B, a position-projection correction can distribute error in proportion to inverse mass:

```text
x_A += n * C * w_A / (w_A + w_B)
x_B -= n * C * w_B / (w_A + w_B)
```

Skip an immovable pair and handle coincident points explicitly. A projection method is useful for learning convergence but is not identical to a velocity-level rigid-body solver. If corrected positions are converted to velocities, corrections can inject energy. Name the algorithm and measure the quantities it actually promises.

### Iterative contact solving
A sequential impulse solver visits constraints, updates velocities locally, and repeats. Contact order affects intermediate results; warm starting reuses prior accumulated impulses to begin closer to a solution. For unilateral normal contact, accumulated normal impulse must remain nonnegative. Compute a proposed change, clamp the accumulated result, then apply only the difference. Otherwise the solver can pull bodies together with an attractive normal force.

Track the maximum and RMS residual across a three-link chain. Record initial positions, timestep, solver iteration count, ordering, gravity and tolerance. Compare 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 iterations, then halve dt. A monotonic trend in one scene is evidence about that setup, not a guarantee for every contact graph. Box2D's documented sub-step count is not a drop-in synonym for every engine's solver-iteration parameter [S02].

### Sweeping through time
At 30 m/s and 60 Hz, a projectile travels 0.5 m each tick. A 0.1 m wall can lie entirely between the starting and ending positions. For a point moving along x with constant velocity v toward a static slab [lo, hi], compute t0 = (lo-x)/v and t1 = (hi-x)/v, sort them, and intersect [t0,t1] with [0,dt]. Initial overlap has a declared hit time of zero in this teaching kernel. Zero velocity outside the slab means no hit. Zero velocity inside means initial overlap.

For an axis-aligned moving box, expand the obstacle by the box's half extents and sweep its center. In several dimensions, intersect the time intervals from each slab. For relative linear motion of two objects, subtract velocities first. Rotation complicates swept bounds and contact geometry; a point-versus-slab result is not general rotational CCD. Library cast APIs may deliberately treat initial overlap differently, which must be recorded in the comparison [S01].

### Worked time of impact
A point starts at x=0 with v=30 m/s; the wall occupies [0.24,0.26] m. Entry occurs at 0.24/30 = 0.008 s and exit at about 0.008667 s. Both occur before the 1/60 s tick ends. The endpoint at 0.5 m is outside the wall, but a sweep detects the entry. With a radius of 0.02 m, expand the wall to [0.22,0.28], so entry is about 0.007333 s.

After finding the first impact, advance to the impact time, solve the collision, and account for the remaining interval according to your policy. Repeated impacts can produce a near-zero-time loop. Bound the number of impacts per tick and specify a conservative fallback, such as stopping the fast body and emitting a diagnostic. Never let a malformed level create unbounded simulation work.

### A disciplined experiment
Implement the swept kernel, then a chain residual experiment. The workbook requires both; a passing slab test does not complete the lesson. Keep raw residual tables rather than only a screenshot. Include a static pair, coincident anchors, a separating projectile, an initial overlap, and an impact exactly at dt. Measure whether more iterations or smaller dt delivers the better error/cost tradeoff in your chosen scene.

For the engine, CCD belongs to selected bodies and motion regimes. It is not a switch that cures all physics failures. Keep a record of which objects use sweeps, which use discrete contacts, and how impact events are scheduled relative to the presentation layer.
extra_questions: A point starts at 0 m and moves at 30 m/s toward the slab [0.24,0.26] m during a 1/60 s tick. What is the entry time, and why does an endpoint test miss it?
A chain becomes less stretchy when solver iterations increase. Does this prove conservation of energy or solve projectile tunneling?
extra_answers: Entry is 0.24/30 = 0.008 s. The final point is at 0.5 m, beyond the slab, so neither endpoint overlaps even though the motion crosses it.
Neither. It shows reduced constraint residual in that experiment. Energy must be measured under the chosen correction model; endpoint collision detection can still miss a between-step crossing.

26.3.transfer: Add a debug CCD flag, a per-tick impact cap and residual telemetry to your engine. Demonstrate that a dense contact scene cannot make one tick loop without a bound.

26.4.body:
### Define exactly what repeatable means
Repeatability is a claim with a scope: same executable and machine; same compiler settings on different machines; or bitwise agreement across named platforms. A visually similar replay is weaker than an identical serialized state. A hash proves agreement only for the bytes you included. Excluding the random generator, an AI cooldown or a spawn counter can make a misleadingly stable hash.

Write a state schema with stable entity IDs, transforms, velocities, gameplay fields, random state and pending deterministic commands. Exclude pointer addresses, padding, wall-clock timestamps and rendering interpolation. Define field order, integer widths, byte order and floating-point representation. Reject NaNs before hashing because NaNs have unusual comparison behavior and multiple bit patterns. Decide how negative zero is treated. Hashes localize differences; they do not make arithmetic deterministic.

### The simulation boundary
Let S_t be the state before tick t. The transition consumes the input bundle I_t and produces S_(t+1) plus an event list E_t. Use an integer tick as the authoritative time index. An accumulator can run zero or more fixed steps per display frame, retaining a previous/current transform pair for rendering interpolation. Cap catch-up work and disclose the overload policy; silently discarding time changes behavior and must not be disguised as successful real-time operation [S19].

Stable iteration order matters when operations are not associative. Three floating-point values can sum differently under different grouping. Thread scheduling, unordered-container traversal and compiler contraction can therefore matter. The current Box2D simulation documentation describes explicit determinism strategies, including creation ordering and compiler assumptions, and warns that deterministic library behavior does not make an entire application deterministic [S02]. Do not repeat the outdated blanket claim that all physics-library cross-platform determinism is impossible.

### Analytic checks expose integration error
For constant acceleration a, an exact one-dimensional reference is x(t)=x0+v0*t+0.5*a*t*t and v(t)=v0+a*t. Semi-implicit Euler updates velocity first and then position. After N equal steps of size h, position is x0+v0*N*h+0.5*a*h*h*N*(N+1). Its position error against the exact solution is 0.5*a*N*h*h, or 0.5*a*t*h. At a=-10 m/s^2, t=1 s and h=1/60 s, error is about -0.083333 m. Halving h should roughly halve this error for this experiment. The expected error is not zero.

A force-free body should maintain velocity. An isolated elastic two-body collision should conserve momentum and kinetic energy within tolerance. A damped system should not be judged by energy conservation. An engine under gravity should not be judged by constant kinetic energy. Write the physical assumptions beside every invariant.

### First-divergence debugging
Run a fixed input tape twice and compare state hashes at every tick. Deliberately alter one input at tick 37. The first differing post-step state should be S_38 under the naming convention above. If only the final hash is stored, hundreds of later contacts obscure the cause. Save the pre-divergence state, the input bundle, candidate/contact order, random state and build metadata. Then compare decoded fields, not just two opaque digest strings.

A serialization round trip is a separate test. Restore a state, advance the same next input, and compare against the unrestored run. Restoration that omits a warm-start cache may preserve visible transforms but change the next tick. Whether such caches belong in a rollback snapshot depends on the engine and the exact determinism goal.

### Engine lifetime and fault policy
Do not destroy physics bodies while iterating the library's event buffer unless the API explicitly permits it. Convert events to stable engine handles, validate generations and enqueue commands for a known safe phase. Renderer interpolation reads snapshots rather than mutable solver storage. Entity deletion should clear presentation ownership without allowing a recycled ID to receive an old collision sound.

On a non-finite value, record the first responsible tick and operation, then stop the test or isolate the body under a documented runtime policy. Replacing every NaN with zero can hide a persistent defect and produce impossible rewards or movement. The full lab combines analytic tests, repeatability, serialization and an adversarial scene suite. This is the evidence foundation for later rollback networking, not an optional debugging convenience.
extra_questions: Using semi-implicit Euler with acceleration -10 m/s^2, zero initial velocity, t=1 s and h=1/60 s, what is the position error against the analytic solution?
Two replay hashes agree, but an omitted AI cooldown differs. What has been proved, and what must change?
extra_answers: The error is 0.5*a*t*h = -5/60 = -0.083333... m. The numerical position is about -5.083333 m rather than -5 m. Halving h halves this error in this constant-acceleration setup.

Only the serialized subset agreed. Include every future-affecting authoritative field, including cooldowns and random state; use explicit schema ordering, then compare the next transition after restore as well as the current snapshot.

27.1.body:
### Coordinate spaces are part of the asset format
An articulated object is a hierarchy, not a bag of independent rotations. Choose column-vector notation for this lesson. A local joint transform maps from the joint's coordinates to its parent's coordinates. The world transform is parent_world * local. A root uses the skeleton's world transform as its parent. Multiplication order is a semantic contract, not a stylistic preference.

Evaluate ancestors before descendants. Imported node order is not necessarily parent-first, so either topologically sort the hierarchy or evaluate recursively with cycle detection and a depth bound. An invalid parent index, a cycle or an excessive depth is malformed asset data. Treat it as a load error rather than letting animation recurse until the stack fails.

### Derive skinning from the bind pose
Let B_j be joint j's world transform in the bind pose and G_j its current world transform, all expressed in compatible spaces. To move a bind-space vertex through joint j, first map it into the joint's bind coordinates with inverse(B_j), then move it into the current pose with G_j. The resulting transform is G_j * inverse(B_j). If the renderer expects positions in mesh-local space, include inverse(mesh_world) on the left. Khronos's skinning tutorial and glTF specification make the joint and inverse-bind relationships explicit [S03, S04].

Linear blend skinning forms a weighted sum of transformed positions:

```text
p_world = sum_j weight_j * G_j * inverse(B_j) * p_bind
sum_j weight_j = 1
```

In the bind pose, G_j=B_j, so each product is identity and the vertex reproduces its original position. This identity test is more valuable than immediately importing a detailed character. Validate finite, nonnegative weights, valid joint indices and a normalization policy. A zero total weight needs an explicit fallback or rejection; division by zero is not an acceptable repair.

### Worked two-joint arm
Joint 0 is at the origin. Joint 1's local translation is (1,0), so its bind world position is (1,0). A vertex bound entirely to joint 1 lies at (2,0) in bind world coordinates. Its joint-local bind position is (1,0). Rotate joint 0 by 90 degrees while preserving joint 1's local translation. Joint 1 moves to (0,1), and the vertex moves to (0,2). Translating each joint independently without inheriting the parent rotation gives the wrong result.

For a blended vertex, use two weights of 0.5. At bind pose, both corrected transforms are identity, so blending still preserves the original vertex. Omitting inverse-bind correction adds the joint's bind placement again and produces displacement even before animation starts. This is a coordinate-space defect, not a bad blend curve.

### Orientation and deformation
Interpolate translation and scale separately from rotation. A quaternion and its negative represent the same orientation; negate one endpoint when their dot product is negative before a shortest-path interpolation. Normalized linear interpolation is useful for small angular differences, while spherical interpolation better preserves constant angular speed between two orientations. Near-equal quaternions need a numerically stable branch. An unnormalized quaternion can introduce invalid transforms.

Linear blend skinning can collapse volume near twists. This is a known model limitation, not always a shader bug. For normals, the transform depends on the skinning and scaling model; nonuniform scale cannot be handled by blindly reusing a position transform. In the core lab, restrict joints to rigid transforms and document that restriction before adding more advanced deformation. Correctness within a declared model is preferable to silently accepting unsupported assets.

### Asset and runtime ownership
Store the immutable hierarchy, bind transforms and clips as resources. Each character owns mutable playback time, blend state and evaluated pose buffers. Sharing a mutable pose across characters can make one actor's animation overwrite another's. The renderer receives a snapshot of joint matrices or a clearly synchronized buffer; it must not read a pose while a job is half finished.

The Python kernel uses 2D transforms to make the parent composition visible. The full lab adds a small skinned mesh or line skeleton to the engine, checks the bind identity, and displays local axes. Test a parent rotation, a translated mesh root, one invalid joint index and a rejected hierarchy cycle. Render at different rates without changing the authoritative animation time. Explain which transforms are local, skeleton-relative, mesh-relative and world-relative in the submission.
extra_questions: A root rotates 90 degrees and its child has local translation (1,0). Where is the child in world coordinates under column-vector parent*local composition?
Why should G_j * inverse(B_j) be identity in the bind pose, and what extra transform is needed for a mesh-local output buffer?
extra_answers: At (0,1), assuming the root is at the world origin. The parent rotation acts on the child translation; adding the unrotated translation would mix spaces.

At bind pose G_j equals B_j, so their product cancels. For mesh-local output, prepend inverse(mesh_world) when G_j and B_j are defined consistently in world space; the exact convention must match the imported asset.

27.1.transfer: Add an immutable skeleton resource and a per-instance pose buffer to the existing engine. Demonstrate two actors sharing one skeleton without sharing playback state.

27.2.body:
### Animation is a controlled state transition
A character does not simply play whichever clip was requested last. Define an animation state machine with entry behavior, exit behavior, interruption rules and transition duration. Idle, walk and action states are enough for this lab. Specify whether an action can be interrupted by movement, damage or pause, and whether a repeated trigger restarts it or is ignored.

Separate state selection from pose evaluation. A transition blends sampled poses, but the gameplay action may have an exact authoritative start tick. The blend's visual midpoint is not automatically the moment a hit occurs. Blend translation and rotation using the conventions from Lesson 27.1. A linear blend parameter rises from 0 to 1 over a declared duration; a smooth curve changes derivative continuity, not the underlying event ownership.

### Phase and root motion
Two walk clips can have compatible speeds but incompatible foot phases. Blending left-foot contact with right-foot contact can produce sliding. Normalize cycle phase or use markers when the asset design requires it. Clip time must have a unit: seconds, normalized cycle fraction or ticks. A variable called time without a unit is a common source of integration mistakes.

Root motion is displacement authored by animation. Physics-driven movement instead derives displacement from simulation. Choose one authority. A useful contract is that animation proposes a displacement, the movement controller resolves collision and accepts a corrected displacement, and the visual pose adapts to the result. Applying both the full authored displacement and the physics velocity double-counts movement. Teleporting a dynamic body to every animation root sample bypasses its physical constraints.

### Derive a two-link inverse-kinematics solution
For a planar arm with lengths L1 and L2 and target (x,y), let d=sqrt(x*x+y*y). The reachable radial range without joint-angle limits is abs(L1-L2) <= d <= L1+L2. The law of cosines gives an elbow angle theta2 through:

```text
c2 = (d*d - L1*L1 - L2*L2) / (2*L1*L2)
theta2 = acos(clamp(c2, -1, 1))
theta1 = atan2(y,x)
         - atan2(L2*sin(theta2), L1+L2*cos(theta2))
```

The negative theta2 branch gives the alternate elbow configuration. A pole direction, previous pose or joint-limit policy selects a branch. Clamp unreachable targets to the reach interval and report that clamping occurred. The clamp on c2 handles small rounding excursions, but it must not conceal an invalid negative link length.

### Worked target and singularity
With L1=L2=1 and target (1,1), d squared is 2, c2=0, theta2=90 degrees and theta1=0 degrees for the chosen branch. Forward kinematics returns (1,1). For target (3,0), the maximum reach is 2, so the arm can extend toward (2,0) but cannot reach (3,0). Reporting a residual of 1 is honest; repeatedly iterating toward an impossible target is wasted computation.

At the origin with equal links, a folded arm can reach the target but the shoulder direction is not uniquely determined. At full extension, small target changes can create large angular changes. Preserve a stable prior direction or use an explicit fallback. In 3D, singularities, joint limits and multiple chains add complexity; this analytic 2D solver is a teaching model rather than a general full-body IK system.

### Ordering the animation pipeline
A typical bounded pipeline samples base clips, blends them, applies an additive layer, solves selected IK constraints, then computes final world transforms. The exact ordering matters. Solving foot IK before an unrelated later layer moves the pelvis can undo the contact. Recompute dependent transforms after local changes. Cache immutable clip data, not partially evaluated mutable poses shared across actors.

Trace each transition with source state, target state, trigger, start tick, blend duration and interruption reason. When a character freezes, the trace should reveal whether a state never exited, a clip time stopped or an IK target became invalid. Do not debug all three through a single final mesh screenshot.

### Deliberate practice
The exercise kernel computes the two-link solution and reports reachability. The full lab must also implement idle/walk/action transitions, cancellation and root-motion ownership. Test target motion across the reach boundary, a pause during a blend, a movement trigger during an action and two consecutive interruptions. Verify pose continuity numerically and inspect behavior at multiple rendering rates. A correct endpoint equation alone does not complete an animation controller.
extra_questions: For links of length 1 and 1 and target (1,1), compute one elbow and shoulder solution. Verify it with forward kinematics.
An action clip moves the root 0.3 m while the physics controller also moves it 0.3 m in the same tick. What contract is missing?
extra_answers: One branch has theta2=pi/2 and theta1=0. The endpoint is (cos(0)+cos(pi/2), sin(0)+sin(pi/2))=(1,1). The other elbow branch is also possible under an appropriate shoulder angle.
Root-motion authority. Animation should either supply a displacement for collision-resolved movement or remain visual while physics supplies movement; adding both gives an unintended 0.6 m step.

27.3.body:
### Audio runs on a different deadline
A sample is one channel's value at one instant. An audio frame contains one sample for every channel. At 48,000 frames per second, 256 stereo frames contain 512 sample values but span only 256/48000 = 0.005333 seconds. Confusing samples, frames and bytes can halve a buffer or overrun it. State the format: sample rate, channel count, sample type and interleaving.

A game may tolerate an occasional long visual frame; the audio device still needs its next buffer. Disk access, memory allocation, waiting on a mutex, console logging and unpredictable callbacks can exceed the available time. PortAudio's callback guidance explicitly cautions against blocking and unpredictable work [S05]. A callback's practical deadline also depends on the platform and buffering arrangement; the buffer duration is a useful budget calculation, not proof of end-to-end latency.

### Generate and mix a signal
A sine oscillator advances phase by 2*pi*frequency/sample_rate each frame. Preserve phase between callbacks or each buffer boundary can introduce a discontinuity. For a mono mix, y[n] = sum_i gain_i*x_i[n]. A conservative no-clipping policy for sources bounded in [-1,1] is sum_i abs(gain_i) <= 1. Two voices at gains 0.25 each have a worst-case peak of 0.5, even when their phases align.

A limiter or soft clipper is a different policy and changes the waveform. Do not call saturation distortion-free. Abrupt gain or playback changes can create clicks; use a short ramp with a specified duration. Choose frequencies below the Nyquist limit, but remember that discontinuous or nonlinear waveforms can introduce harmonics above it. The core lab uses generated tones so no third-party assets or codecs are needed.

### Bounded work and ownership
Keep a fixed-size voice array. A callback processes at most a declared number of control commands and at most the configured voice count times the output frame count. Even a lock-free queue can be abused by draining until empty while the producer keeps filling it. Bound commands per callback. If the queue fills, drop or coalesce noncritical updates under an explicit policy and count the event outside the callback.

A single-producer/single-consumer ring has one writer for its write index and one writer for its read index. The producer writes a slot before publishing the new write index with release ordering. The consumer observes that index with acquire ordering before reading the slot. Slot reuse requires the reverse publication of the read index. This ownership pattern does not extend automatically to multiple producers. The native C++ companion makes these boundaries concrete and checks whether its atomic index type is lock-free on the build target.

Allocate and decode before playback. Pass stable handles or immutable sample buffers to audio, not pointers to resources that the game thread may immediately free. A stop command must be acknowledged or otherwise synchronized before resource reclamation. An audio callback should not depend on a renderer lock or gameplay allocation to finish.

### Worked budget and stress test
Suppose the chosen device consumes 256-frame buffers at 48 kHz. An illustrative measured callback cost of 0.7 ms leaves about 4.63 ms relative to the buffer duration. That is not a guarantee against scheduling delays. Record maximum observed callback time, distribution, underrun count if exposed, voice count and the measurement method. Never invent an underrun count when the API does not expose one; report the available observation and its limitation.

The native harness times offline callback invocations, so it can test arithmetic, bounded command processing and queue behavior. It does not prove that a real device is underrun-free. The full lesson requires the learner to connect a maintained platform API, mix two tones, vary gains and run a deadline-stress test. SDL3 stream callbacks have their own thread and API contracts; consult the selected SDL3 page rather than copying SDL2 callback code [S06].

### Completion boundary
The Python exercise creates offline samples to verify phase continuity and gain bounds. Python execution is not presented as a real-time audio callback implementation. The C++ harness demonstrates a native ownership pattern without linking a device library. Actual hardware playback, mute/device-loss behavior and callback stress evidence remain required lab work. Start at low output volume and avoid testing with unexpectedly loud peaks. Preserve separate music/effects settings and a master mute for the next lesson.
extra_questions: How many sample values are in 256 stereo frames, and what duration do they represent at 48 kHz?
Why can draining a lock-free command queue until empty still violate a callback deadline? Give a bounded alternative.
extra_answers: There are 512 sample values, but the duration is 256/48000 seconds, about 5.333 ms. Channel count changes storage, not the number of time instants.

A producer can keep adding work, and each command may have a nontrivial cost. Limit commands per callback, cap voices and output frames, and define overflow/coalescing behavior. Lock-free does not mean bounded total callback work.
